description: Person(s) authorized to work with management representatives in support of water efficiency activities (A.6: may be one person in small organizations).
Risks and opportunities to be addressed for the WEMS (§6.1 a)-e)); documented information maintained (§6.1 i, ii).
Measurable water efficiency objectives at relevant functions and levels, consistent with the policy (§6.2.1 a)-f); 3.19).
What will be done to achieve each objective.
What resources will be required to achieve the objective.
Who will be responsible for achieving the objective.
When the objective will be completed.
How the results of the objective will be evaluated.
Water efficiency planning process(es) implemented and documented.
Plan detailing locations of water use, recycling potential, water-saving measures and an action plan (§6.2.2 a)-d); 3.34).
Legal requirements or other requirements considered and reviewed at defined intervals (3.14).
Review determining water efficiency performance from data, identifying improvement opportunities (§6.2.4 a)-d); 3.40).
Current water sources identified during water-use analysis (incl. drinking water and reclaimed/alternative water).
Activities/functions of significant water use, incl. facilities, equipment, systems, processes, personnel and other variables (3.28).
Evaluated past and present water use from measurement and other data.
Estimated future water use.
Measure of business activity specific to the application site, e.g. units produced, staff/visitors, guestrooms (3.4; Annex D).
Numeric value of the selected business activity indicator (units, persons, guestrooms, etc.).
Amount of water used per unit of business activity indicator, e.g. m3 water/kg product; l/person; m3/guestroom (3.33).
Reference level of water used per business activity indicator; changes measured against it (3.2).
Trigger requiring baseline adjustment (§6.2.7 a)-c)).

enum_values.label_de: Indikator spiegelt Wassernutzung nicht mehr wider
enum_values.label_en: Business activity indicator(s) no longer reflect organizational water use

enum_values.label_de: Änderungen an Prozess, Betriebsmustern oder Wassersystemen
enum_values.label_en: Changes to process, operational patterns or water systems
Variation from predetermined and documented methods

description: Data period suitable to the organization's water use for establishing/computing indicators (A.7.5).
Water efficiency targets at relevant functions, levels, processes or facilities.
Time frame established for achievement of the target.
Action plan incl. responsibility, means/time frame, improvement-verification method and result-verification method (§6.3 1)-4)).
Method by which an improvement in water efficiency performance shall be verified.
Resources determined and provided for establishment, implementation, maintenance and continual improvement of the WEMS.
Necessary competence of person(s) whose work affects water efficiency performance, ensured by education/training/experience (3.5).
Appropriate documented information retained as evidence of competence.
Persons under the organization's control are aware of policy, roles, contribution, impacts and implications (§7.3 a)-e)).
Internal/external communications determined: what, when, with whom, how (§7.4 a)-d)), plus a suggestions process.
Documented information required by the standard and determined necessary by the organization (3.9).
Documented information controlled for availability, protection, distribution, storage, change control and retention/disposal (§7.5.3 a)-b), 1)-4)).
Processes planned/implemented/controlled with criteria; changes and outsourced processes controlled (§8.1 a)-c), 1)-2)).
Criteria for processes incl. minimum levels for effective management of significant water use.
Water efficiency improvement opportunities and operational control considered in design of new/modified/renovated facilities; documented.
Criteria for assessing water use/efficiency over operating lifetime when procuring services, products and equipment; documented purchasing specifications.
Suppliers informed that procurement is partly evaluated on the basis of water efficiency performance.
Water-consuming facilities/equipment/systems/processes maintained and inspected on a regular basis.
Water supplied by a water utility to the site (input term; denominator term in recycling-rate formulae).
Other water source input stream 1 (e.g. sea water, ground water, reclaimed water, rain water).
Other water source input stream 2.
Other water source input stream 3.
Water output stream 1 (e.g. evaporation/drift, water in products, irrigation, discharge, losses).
Water output stream 2.
Water output stream 3.
Water output stream 4.
Total water input = WD + R1 + R2 + R3 (Formula C.1/C.2).
Total water output = O1 + O2 + O3 + O4 (Formula C.1/C.2). Win > Wout indicates leaks/uncontrolled losses.
Total reused/recycled water from the process (Formulae C.3, C.5 where-clause).

label_en: Reused/recycled water not from the process
description: Total reused/recycled water not from the process (Formula C.3 where-clause).
Incoming water to process (Formula C.5 where-clause).

label_en: Reused/recycled water from process back to process
description: Reused/recycled water from process back to process (Formula C.5 where-clause).
Plant/premises recycling rate (%) over all reused/reclaimed streams = (Rp + Rnp) / (Rp + Rnp + WD) * 100 (Formula C.3).
Process recycling rate (%) over process streams only = Rp / (Wp + Rpp) * 100 (Formula C.5).
Determination of what/how/when to monitor, measure, analyse and evaluate (§9.1 a)-d)).
As a minimum, the water use shall be metered (3.38 water meter).

Minimum monitored items: water types by source, significant water use, relevant variables, business activity indicators, water efficiency indicators, action-plan effectiveness, actual vs. expected use.
Significant deviations in water efficiency performance identified and investigated.
Evaluation of compliance with legal/other requirements (water use, efficiency, wastewater discharge, pollution control).
Internal audits conducted at planned intervals to check WEMS conformity and effective implementation (3.1).
Audit programme planned/established/implemented/maintained incl. frequency, methods, responsibilities and reporting (§9.2.2 a)-e)).
Top management reviews the WEMS at planned intervals considering §9.3 a)-d); outputs/decisions per 1)-5).
Non-fulfilment of a requirement; reacted to and evaluated for cause (3.18; §10.1 a)-b)).
Action to eliminate the cause of a nonconformity and prevent recurrence, appropriate to its effects (3.8; §10.1 c)-e)).
Organization continually improves suitability, adequacy and effectiveness of the WEMS using evaluation and review outputs (3.7).
Principal purpose of the sampling programme: quality control, quality characterization, or pollution-source identification per the §1 scope (incl. water, sediments and sludge); elaborated in §3.
Matrix to be characterized: water, sediment or sludge (§1 scope explicitly includes sediments and sludge).
Confirmation the applicable normative references were consulted (ISO 5667/2, 5667/3, ISO 6107/1, 6107/2, ISO 2602, ISO 3534).
Programme objectives established before designing the programme, since they govern site position, frequency, duration, procedures, post-treatment and analytical requirements.
Preliminary site visit to verify sampling points, gather preliminary/secondary information, define procedures and run preliminary sampling/analysis before final objectives are set.
All relevant data from previous programmes at the same or similar locations and other local-condition information taken into account.
Compiled list of parameters of interest (physical, chemical, biological, radiological) with relevant analytical procedures consulted.
General requirements (§4.1, order-of-magnitude levels/loads) vs specific requirements (§4.2, detailed levels/load distributions).

Specific sub-objective from the §4.2 a)-r) catalogue (e.g. water-use suitability, wastewater-discharge effect, treatment performance, estuary mixing, industrial loss, boiler/recovered water, cooling control, atmospheric rainwater, land inputs, sediment release, river regulation, distribution-quality change, hydrological dynamics, aquatic ecology, environmental baseline).
Expected variability of the determinand: stable (simple programme), slow/not-marked, or wide/rapid variations (complex programme).
Sampling at or near system boundaries avoided unless those conditions are of special interest.
Requirements of applicable safety regulations taken into account and sampling staff informed of necessary precautions.
Life-jackets and life-lines used when sampling large water bodies; weather conditions considered.
Before entering confined spaces, oxygen concentration and any toxic vapour/gas measured; breathing/resuscitation/protective equipment available.
Work procedures, site design and equipment maintenance planned to minimize electrocution risk with electrically operated equipment in/near water.
Sampling network extent, from a single site to a whole river drainage; key-station flow measurement customary (see Section Four).
Sampling location identified for comparable resampling (riverbank features, static objects, instrumental methods, map references).
Flow character: ideally turbulent well-mixed liquid (induce turbulence in pipes), except for dissolved-gas/volatile determinands; account for change over time and reverse flow.
For heterogeneous liquids pumped through pipes, minimum nominal bore 25 mm at high linear velocity to maintain turbulent flow; avoid horizontal pipe runs.
For suspended-solids determination, sample under isokinetic conditions (per ISO 6107/2) with adequate mixing/turbulence, or across the full flow cross-section.
For volatile content, pump with minimal suction force; keep all tubing full; draw the sample from a pressurized pipe after purging some material.
Changes in meteorological conditions recorded and accounted for when interpreting results.
Practical sampling situation determining site-selection guidance (natural waters 9, industrial 10, commercial effluents 11, wastewater 12, stormwater 13).
Well pumped before sampling to draw fresh water from the aquifer; wells near corrodible materials fully pumped to remove accumulated corrosion products.
Depth below ground level at which the groundwater sample is taken always recorded.
Where the purpose is to control discharge effects, sample upstream and downstream, considering mixing of discharge and receiving water; extend downstream an appropriate distance.
Cooling-system type: open evaporative, once-through (free-pass), or closed circuit -- determines sampling points.
For safety, manholes designed so commercial-effluent sampling can be done without entering.
When sampling sludge from a pipe, the sampling conduit shall be at least 50 mm diameter to minimize blockages; sample at frequent intervals.
For raw wastewater, two or three routine samples at different points mixed into a composite sample where composition varies across the sewer.
Where automatic samplers are upstream of preliminary processes, a screen or small macerator is added at the sampler inlet to prevent blockages; stormwater heterogeneity considered.
For stormwater/surface runoff, flow-proportional sampling is desirable; flow-started automatic samplers kept in permanent readiness; rainfall & air temperature recorded.
Programme type: quality control (control within defined limits), quality characterization (estimate statistical parameters), or pollution-cause investigation.
Defined limits within which the determinand concentration is controlled (quality-control programmes); frequency set by magnitude/duration and probability of deviations.
Statistical parameter to be estimated in a characterization programme: arithmetic mean / median (central tendency) or standard deviation (variability).
Sampling frequency increased while abnormal conditions persist (plant start-up, river flood, algal bloom); such results used in long-term trends only if increased frequency is foreseen.

Long sampling-occasion duration / composite sampling used when only average quality over a period matters and the determinand is stable, reducing analytical work at the expense of variation knowledge.
Individual measured result x_i used to estimate the mean and standard deviation.
Arithmetic mean of the n individual results (estimate of the true mean).
Number of samples/results; required number for a target confidence interval = (2Ksigma/L)^2 (Eq.3). Worked example -> n approx 61.
Estimate of the standard deviation from n results (Eq.1); used in place of sigma when sigma is unknown.
Standard deviation of the distribution; required for the confidence interval and number-of-samples formulae (use s when sigma is unknown).
Probability (%) that the true arithmetic mean lies within the calculated confidence interval L; selects K from the §16.4 table.
Confidence interval of the mean of n results at a given confidence level; L=2Ksigma/sqrt(n) (Eq.2); a target L drives the required n (Eq.3).
Aspect of flow to be measured: direction (§19.2), velocity (§19.3), or discharge rate (§19.4).
Flow direction: unidirectional (most inland watercourses) or variable (navigable/drainage channels, estuaries; groundwater direction for aquifer pollution).
Current velocity, used to calculate discharge rate, mean velocity/travel time, and to assess turbulence/mixing.
Discharge rate = volume of liquid passing a point per unit time; mean and extreme values essential for design/operation and rational quality limits.
Method used to measure flow direction/velocity/discharge (discrete or continuous), per the §21.1-21.4 catalogue; practical detail per ISO/TC 30 & ISO/TC 113.
Measurement mode: discrete (e.g. floats, direct-reading current meter) or continuous (most discharge flow meters).

Discharge type: planned discharge (3.7: subject to prior agreement against predefined parameters/limit values) or permanent discharge (3.8: continuous direct discharge, not under agreement but conforming to limit values).
Form of waste water to be sampled within the scope: industrial, radioactive, cooling, raw domestic or treated domestic waste water.
Confirmation the applicable normative references were consulted (ISO 5667-1, -3, -7, -14, -16; ISO 6107 all parts; ISO 19458).
Defined sample type per clause 3: composite sample (3.1), grab sample (3.3), or qualified grab sample (3.4: >=5 grab samples mixed within <=2 h, intervals >=2 min).
Number of grab samples forming a qualified grab sample: at least five, taken and mixed within a maximum period of two hours and at intervals not less than two minutes.
Maximum period over which the >=5 grab samples of a qualified grab sample are taken and mixed: two hours.
Minimum interval between the grab samples of a qualified grab sample: not less than two minutes.

A detailed sampling strategy (often based on a preliminary survey identifying the important aspects) is established; both objective and environmental situation determine how sampling is carried out (general design per ISO 5667-1).
Representativeness notion by medium: in a flow (channel, sewer, manhole, pressure pipe) or in storage (tank, lagoon, basin); each treated differently.
Sampling carried out in sections where the flow is well-mixed and homogeneous, representative of the waste stream to be examined.

Each sampling point documented: identification, site location, photos, geographic coordinates, flow type (open/closed), access conditions and sampling technique; candidate points identified from sewer plans then verified in situ.
Flow type recorded for the sampling point: open or closed conduit.

For points with a fixed automatic sampling device: vehicle access, level work surfaces, lighting/electrical connection, water connection for cleaning, adequate safety precautions (railings/fall-arrest) and flow meters for flow-dependent sampling are provided.

If hydraulic conditions do not ensure representativeness (no flow, reduced activity, abnormal load increase), the unusual situation is noted in the sampling report and the client & analysis laboratory informed.
Number of samples to take during each period, decided by statistical techniques (ISO 2602, ISO 3534 all parts, ISO 5667-1) or often by the regulator/pollution-control authority.
Random number A used in the sampling-day/week formulae: for Formula 1 in the interval -365/n .. 0, for Formula 2 in the interval -52/n .. 0.
Index k = 1, 2, ..., n enumerating successive sampling occasions in the sampling-day/week formulae.
Day of the year on which the k-th sample shall be taken, A + 365*k/n (Formula 1); applies for n greater than about 25.
Week number during which the k-th sample shall be taken, A + 52*k/n (Formula 2); applies for n smaller than about 25; the weekday is chosen so all days of the week are covered.
Source of quality variation taken into account when timing sampling: diurnal (a), day-of-week (b), week/month (c), seasonal (d), stormwater-episode (e) variations or trends (f).
Where identifying the nature/magnitude of peak load is important, sampling limited to the day/week/month periods when peak loads are known to occur.
Length of the monitoring/sampling period: a year, several months/weeks, or even shorter periods; the chosen period shall cover any seasonal variation.
Specific-site category determining site guidance: sewers/channels/manholes (5.1), wastewater-treatment plant (5.2), industrial site (5.3) or cooling-water system (5.4).
Recommended sampling depth below the surface in sewers/channels: generally between one-third and one-half of the effluent water depth, at a minimum distance from bed and walls.
The sampling point is downstream of any flow restriction and, as a rule, at least three times the pipe diameter (or channel width) downstream of the restriction.
WWTP sampling objective: whole-plant performance (samples at main inlet & outlet) or individual-unit / unit-group control (samples at the unit inlet & outlet).
Relevance of any bypass flow and the need to sample it assessed, as it may be necessary for the sample to be representative of the overall effluent.
Cooling-water system type determining sampling points: once-through (continuous flow), coupled primary/secondary circuits (sample on the return side), or closed cooling.
At a cooling-water sampling installation the water is allowed to run for at least 30 s before sampling.
The cooling-water sampling point is located upstream of the biocide dosing point so results are not distorted by biocide dosing.
Principal waste-water sampling type selected: grab sampling (6.1) or composite sampling (6.2).
Grab-sampling method: direct in laboratory bottles, ballasted collector with bottles, automatic sampler (direct), sampling rod with collection vessel (indirect), or bucket/other equipment (indirect).

Composite-sampling mode: CVVT (constant-volume/variable-time, flow-proportional), CTVV (constant-time/variable-volume, flow-proportional), CTCV (constant-time/constant-volume, time-proportional) or manual composite (fixed time/flow/volume).

Maximum tolerated deviation between two measurements of the selected parameter to satisfy the homogeneity criterion: preferably below 20 % (also for downstream-sampling validation during the whole discharge).
The client clearly defines the sampling objective so the operator applies the appropriate sampling strategy.
Sampling-line length at least five times the pipe diameter from the collector to ensure sampling in the fully mixed zone; avoid long horizontal runs.
Interval between individual discrete samples for discontinuous composite sampling: <=5 min for a 2 h mixed sample and <=30 min for a 24 h mixed sample.
Automatic-sampler suction/outlet tube internal diameter shall be greater than or equal to 9 mm.
Suction velocity shall not be lower than 0,5 m/s to avoid segregation of suspended matter in the sampling loop; a velocity of 0,3 m/s is acceptable where the internal diameter is 12 mm or more.
Unit volume adequate for representative sampling: at least 50 ml for the vacuum pump or 25 ml for the inline piston.
Sampling bias of the automatic sampler unit volume shall not exceed 10 %.
Repeatability of the automatic sampler unit volume shall not exceed 5 % (typical CoV <=5 % at a 250 ml volume; smaller volumes validated before use).
Resulting flow uncertainty U (k=2) shall not exceed 15 % (see Annex I).
For flow-proportional composite sampling (CVVT/CTVV) the automatic sampler is connected to a flow meter (closed-conduit electromagnetic/ultrasonic or open-channel sensors).
Vfinal: total volume (ml) of the laboratory bottles, used in Formula 3 to reconstitute a flow-related mean.
M3total: total discharged volume (m3) over the composite period, used in Formula 3.

label_en: Discharged volume for bottle n M3n
description: M3n: volume discharged during the sampling of bottle n (m3), used in Formula 3.

label_en: Sample volume for bottle n Vn
description: Vn: volume (ml) to take from bottle n = Vfinal x (M3n/M3total) (Formula 3); reconstitutes a flow-related mean from a multi-bottle time-proportional automatic composite.
Unless otherwise specified, grab sampling in an effluent stream is done about 30 cm below the surface or at mid water column in a homogeneous zone, to avoid the surface film and sediments.
Automatic, remote-start or event-triggered sampling based on real-time on-line monitoring of waste-water parameters, triggered when a predetermined criterion is met (defined term per §3.10).

For planned-discharge cistern sampling, tank content mixed for an operator-defined period and mixing maintained during sampling, with no effluent allowed to flow into the tank between start and end of sampling until end of authorized discharge.
Equipment-material nature chosen for compatibility with the target parameter and to ensure absence of physico-chemical interference (Annex E).

For low-concentration parameters, avoid materials with brass connections, pigmented (coloured) plastic and non-food chlorinated PVC (release metals/organics); if used, demonstrate absence of contamination/adsorption (see 10.3).
Automatic sampler may be fixed or portable (and may be equipped with a refrigerated chamber).

Automatic sampler keeps samples in an enclosed dark compartment at a temperature compatible with ISO 5667-3 preservation for the whole sampling duration; portable non-refrigerated allowed only by agreement with the client.
Pumping-system technology of the automatic sampler: vacuum pump (VAP), peristaltic pump (PP), inline piston, or external pumping system (advantages/disadvantages in Annex F).
Manual sampling equipment volume adequate for representative sampling: at least 25 ml.
When manual samples are used to prepare composites, the bottle/vessel/bucket volume is well-defined and known and the repeatability coefficient of variation is within +/-5 %.

Before sampling the equipment is cleaned (Annex C) and checked (10.3); rinsed appropriately, but not rinsed in the waste water where this would influence subsequent analyses (oils/greases, raw/final effluents, microbiology).

Tank mixing system to homogenize content before discharge: one or more mechanical agitators, overpressure bubbling (e.g. compressed air), or forced recirculation (nozzle/pump); effective without re-stratification, for a predefined duration.

Tank sampling device: valved sampling pipe collecting away from the inner wall (avoid surface/edge/bottom), several pipes at different heights, a ballasted self-sealing sampler, or a by-pass on a recirculation line; inert materials.
Where multiple extractions or several bottles are filled from one sample, the sample is homogenized (in situ or in the laboratory) with a validated method whose effectiveness is checked.
For larger collected volumes (e.g. >5 l) transportable mechanical/magnetic-stirrer homogenizers should be used; for volumes <=5 l the laboratory method (manual agitation, rod mixing) may be applied.
Collected sample volume; determines the homogenization method (mechanical for >5 l, laboratory method for <=5 l).
Bottle type, pre-treatments (acidification, alkalinization, freezing, labelling agents) and preservation/handling carried out per ISO 5667-3, defined jointly with the laboratory.
Maximum storage time between sampling and analysis, set per ISO 5667-3/16/19458; any deviation justified and agreed between the sampling body, laboratory and client.
Between sampling and reception, samples stored in a refrigeration device maintaining (5 +/- 3) C; on reception stored per ISO 5667-3/16/19458.

The sampling operator ensures security and traceability of samples, sub-samples and records; any loss/damage in transport recorded; couriers keep similar records (more onerous rules may apply for legal samples).

When an automatic sampler is used, traceability also records: equipment identification, programming, parametric use conditions, material cleaning (yes/no), suction-tube diameter (mm) & length (m), suction velocity, line purge (yes/no), strainer use (yes/no), total volume collected and observations.
A history of changes to sampling protocols/procedures (methods, points, personnel) is maintained so reviewers can assess their impact on the data series.
Specific written instructions on contamination-avoidance protocols provided to sampling personnel; deviations documented; intermediate materials limited and effectively rinsed if used.
Single-use powder-free nitrile gloves used for all sampling and conditioning operations to avoid contamination.

All information reported on the field form: environmental conditions, discharge aspects, contaminants, anomalies and precise coordinates/location; bottles labelled clearly and unambiguously before further samples are taken.
Samples identified by a pre-printed site label with a unique machine-readable code duplicated on the sample label and the laboratory sample-record document.

Quality assurance and control of waste-water sampling carried out per ISO 5667-14; all sample-contacting material subject to QC for contamination/analyte loss; equipment checked (Annex H) and non-conformities recorded.

The sampling/analytical report records all conditions influencing results: date/time (+ completion for composite), operator identity, exact site/point identification & location, number of elementary samples, sampling type, in-situ physico-chemical measurements, QC applied & type, preservation/filtration/storage information, deviations and relevant observations.
The risk associated with sampling is considered before any sampling is carried out; this document does not replace local/national rules; safety is shared by client, sampling agency and subcontractor.
PPE used systematically for all sampling operations: safety shoes/boots, helmet, goggles, disposable gloves and handling gloves to protect from toxic/pathogenic exposure.
Hazard-dependent PPE available as required: emergency/gas masks, gas detector (H2S, CO, O2), safety harness, tripod, fall arrest, lone-worker alarm, chemical-resistant gloves.

Where specific risks exist, the sampling operation is carried out by two persons to ensure safety and raise the alarm; if access/safety conditions are not met, sampling is not performed and the client & laboratory are informed.

Fixed/automatic equipment protected from natural hazards, theft and vandalism and posing no risk to environment/public; confined-space and water-level precautions observed; ATEX-compliant intrinsically-safe equipment used in potentially explosive atmospheres.
Origin/type of the sludge to be sampled: waste-water treatment works, water-treatment works, septic-tank sludges, or industrial process (slurries = water+solids of natural/artificial processes).
Confirmation the purpose covered by this part (design of the sampling programme and collection of samples for sludges of all types and all stages) has been established.
Confirmation the applicable normative references were consulted: ISO 5667-15 (preservation & handling of sludge & sediment samples) and ISO 6107 (vocabulary).
Per the §1 WARNING: appropriate safety & health practices established and applicable regulatory limitations complied with before applying this standard.
Physical form of the sludge: liquid sludge (flowing under gravity/pressure below a certain threshold, 3.8) or sludge cake (generated from dewatering devices, 3.15).
Point, step or procedure at which control can be applied and is essential to prevent or eliminate a hazard or reduce it to an acceptable level (3.3).
Point, step or procedure at which control can be applied and is important or even critical for acceptable quality, but not necessarily for safety (3.12).
Number of sites: one of the variables (with number of replicates and sampling frequency) determining the variability captured; estimated & vetted against data-quality requirements.

Objective of the sampling programme determining the type of analysis: monitoring for process control (in-line instrumentation) or quality control (consult CEN/TR 13097 for hazard analysis & critical/quality control points).
Stage(s) included in the sampling programme: influent monitoring, in-process monitoring, effluent monitoring, and equipment inspection & testing.
Whether the maximum concentration or the average concentration of a pollutant is required; this depends on the variability of discharge and governs the sampling design.
Type of variation in wastewater due to process variability: daily/weekly (scheduled processes/cleaning), seasonal (large load changes), or event (e.g. rainfall increasing volume).
Whether fixed-point sampling requires permanent equipment installation; verify any equipment is regularly cleaned & free from corrosion.
The laboratory performing the examination consulted before installation of fixed-point equipment or implementation of a new sampling scheme (to assess interference & test results).

Equipment chosen for the situation (as simple as practical): manual, automatic sampler for liquids (Annex A), vacuum sampling device (Annex B), or apparatus for sampling from pipes under pressure (Annex C).
Sampling equipment robust, free of contaminating influence, and kept clean & free from corrosion so it does not affect the sample composition.

Container material chosen with care: double polyethylene bags (cake); polyethylene/polypropylene/polycarbonate/glass (liquids); glass preferred for organic constituents but not for trace metals (e.g. mercury) -- prefer polyethylene. See ISO 5667-15.
For trace-metals & moisture determination, containers should be air-tight to prevent leakage/ingress and reduce moisture loss by evaporation.
Specific guidance on containers and sample preservation obtained from ISO 5667-15 (incl. material-vs-determinand suitability and preservatives).
Where automatic sampling is installed, replicate samples taken (alternately into containers A and B) to establish the confidence that the data is representative.

Replicate sampling regime: 10 replicate samples taken for every 40 ordinary samples (1 in 20 sampled), and a further 10 if the regime changes, to statistically test sampling performance before any decision to alter the regime.

Basic sample type: a composite sample (generated from continuous or grab samples from stockpiles, sampling liquid or cake) or a grab sample (random from a liquid/conveyor flow of cake or from a single point in a stockpile).
Sampling mode: time-basis (interval t), continuous (uniform throughout supply), intermittent/consignment (proportion of batches), or flow-related (extracting a mass proportional to flow rate).
Mass of the batch in tonnes, used to compute the time-basis sampling interval t (Equation 1).
Maximum mass flow rate in tonnes per hour, used to compute the time-basis sampling interval t (Equation 1).
Maximum sampling interval (minutes) between taking samples when using time-based sampling; t = 60m/(qn) (Equation 1).
Number of samples; appears as input to the time-basis interval (Eq.1) and as the minimum sub-sample number for a composite sample n=(1,96 s/E)^2 (Eq.2, 95 % confidence).
Standard deviation estimated from test sampling (repeated collection & analysis of >=30 grab samples at plant set-up, checked at intervals); input to the composite sub-sample number (Eq.2).
Maximum permitted error, expressed in the same units as s; input to the composite sub-sample number (Eq.2). Annex D example: E = +/-30 mg/kg dry mass.

Source/location from which the sludge is sampled, determining the technique: tanks & road tankers (6.3.3), pipes (6.3.4), open channels (6.3.5), heaps & stockpiles (6.3.6), wagons (6.3.7), conveyor belts (6.3.8), long piles (6.3.9), after dewatering by centrifugation (6.3.10).

For liquid sludges of low solids content, a relatively large volume of sampled material collected for a truly representative analysis (quantities consulted with the analyst); homogenized before sub-sampling.

Solids content of the sludge; for open-channel sampling a solids content of up to 5 % mass fraction can be sampled, provided velocity in the suction pipe is sufficient; above this a composite may be needed.
Samples should be taken across the width and depth of the channel/heap to ensure representativeness (e.g. weighted bucket or pump across the full depth in open channels).
Nominal volume of the heap/stockpile in cubic metres; input to the number-of-sub-samples formula n_sp = sqrt(V)/2 (Equation 3).
Number of sub-samples for a heap/stockpile composite; n_sp = sqrt(V)/2 (Eq.3), rounded to the nearest whole number and constrained between 4 and 30.
For major variations through stockpiles (e.g. old ones with anaerobic/aerobic layering), core sampling preferred where it can be safely undertaken to enable representative sampling.
Whether the bulk solid sample mass must be reduced to a representative laboratory/test sample; reduction carried out so the sample at each stage stays representative of the original.
Sample thoroughly mixed, coned on a clean flat hard surface, flattened, divided into quarters; diametrically opposed quarters retained & combined; repeated until sufficiently reduced.
For gelatinous/heavy material or to obtain multiple sub-samples, riffle boxes / spinning rifflers used; riffle-box openings of nominal size at least 4x the largest material particle (Figure 1).

When two or more laboratory samples are required, all excess rejected bulk recombined at each division stage, mixed thoroughly and reduced again to provide each further laboratory sample (e.g. laboratory duplicates).

Whether the analytical technique is time-dependent (e.g. pH change over time); judgements on acceptable loss of statistical confidence made on a situation-specific basis; analyse as soon as possible after collection.

For some liquid sludges (raw sewage, rags), gross atypical solids removed by passing the sample through a stainless-steel/plastics screen of nominal openings not less than 5 mm (caution re trace metals/biocide for plastics).

Samples stored until all data obtained & checked, in containers appropriate to the analyte(s) with preservatives added if necessary; storage duration & conditions per ISO 5667-15:2009, Table 1; seek specific guidance from the receiving analyst.

Relevant safety regulations observed when selecting sampling locations & sampling (sewer/treatment-works risks, potentially hazardous sludge); safety guidance per ISO 5667-10:1992 Clause 6; local/national health & safety regulations not substituted.
Sample containers clearly & unambiguously marked; all details relevant to the sample recorded on an attached label so results can be properly interpreted.

Detail considered for inclusion in the sample record (a-h): identification; sampling site (locatable); date & time; sampler name; weather; appearance; preservation technique used; specific storage requirements.
Objective of the study, which governs the choice of representative sampling points, frequency, type of samples and the suitability of the biotest (elaborated in §3.1).
Type of biological test to be performed: toxicity, biodegradation, bioaccumulation or genotoxicity (emphasis on single-species ecotoxicological tests; bacteriological examination excluded).
Confirmation the applicable normative references were consulted: ISO 5667-3 (preservation & handling of samples) and ISO 5667-10 (sampling of waste waters).
Representative sampling points, frequency and sample type chosen according to the study objective; sampling approach compatible with the biotest purpose.
When dividing a bulk sample into portions, homogeneity maintained during subsampling (continuous shaking/stirring), particularly for two-phase mixtures (suspended particulates, algal suspensions).
Material of vessels/containers: chemically inert, easily cleaned, resistant to heating & freezing -- glassware, polyethene or polytetrafluoroethene (PTFE) recommended.
Total sample volume taken, sufficient for supplementary or repeated testing; small volumes preferred to minimize freezing/thawing time -- generally no more than 10 l.
Whether containers are filled completely to the brim or only partially, accounting for sample type, preservation and biotest envisaged; samples for freezing not filled completely (volume expansion).
Samples protected against breakage, temperature increase and external contamination during transport; waterproof markers/labels used to avoid misidentification of samples transported in melting ice.
Maximum storage time at ambient temperature (max 25 C) shall not exceed 12 h; samples processed preferably without delay.
Use of biocidal preservatives excluded for biotesting; addition of highly concentrated acids/bases to stabilize the sample (HCl, NaOH) not recommended.
Technical equipment materials chemically inert with no foreign matter (plasticizers) and no organism growth; glass/PTFE preferred; copper, copper alloy and non-inert plastics not suitable.

Surfaces silanized to minimize adsorption: 5 % dimethyldichlorosilane solution in chloroform or n-heptane, solvent evaporated, heated to 180 C for 2 h; not used for highly adsorbable substances or PTFE.
Silanizing solution: dimethyldichlorosilane at a volume fraction of 5 % in chloroform or n-heptane.
Storage temperature: cool to 0-5 C (storage up to 24 h, ISO 5667-10) or deep-freeze below -18 C; max ambient temperature 25 C.
Preparatory step used to make the test sample from the sample, per Figure 1: dissolving, homogenizing, sedimenting, filtering, neutralizing, aerating.
Frozen samples thawed immediately before use in running water or a warm water bath at a temperature not exceeding 25 C, with gentle shaking, avoiding local overheating; completely thawed before use.

Homogenization method to ensure even distribution of soluble & particulate components (gentle agitation, vigorous shaking, ultrasonic treatment, high-speed dispersion), chosen by volatile-loss potential; original status altered as little as possible.
Pore size of the sterilization-grade membrane used to remove bacteria/organisms (e.g. 0,2 um membrane filtration); high risk of side effects.
Coarse filtration to remove large particulate matter: a coarse filtration (>50 um) is recommended, removing only gross particles before any finer filtration.
Relative centrifugal force used to separate particulate matter, e.g. 10 min at 4500 g +/- 1500 g (i.e. 3000-6000 g).
Sedimentation/settlement time before decanting, e.g. 30 min to 2 h, to remove only gross particles.

pH to which the sample is adjusted: to the pH of the receiving water, or to a defined pH between 6 and 9 (usually tolerable for aquatic biota); neutralization without exceeding the tolerance, avoiding passing the neutral point.
Water solubility of the substance; a solubility of less than approximately 100 mg/l is considered sparingly soluble, requiring special preparation methods.

Method/aid for poorly soluble substances: sonication, temperature increase, addition of acids/bases, dissolution in a volatile/miscible solvent, solubilizing agent (concentration <0,1 g/l), sorption on an inert carrier (per ISO 10634), ultrasonic treatment (20 kHz, 30 min), or emulsifying agent (<=100 mg/l).
Emulsifying agents used at a mass concentration of <=100 mg/l should be non-toxic and stable throughout the test period.
Continuous or intermittent aeration provided in special cases to supply oxygen for test animals & heterotrophic microorganisms, while avoiding stripping of volatiles and substance loss by foaming.
pH adjusted & controlled during the test where it drifts; abiotic pH drift distinguished using a control batch without organisms.

Dilution water/medium: deionized water cannot be used; chlorine-free tapwater, synthetic fresh water (with nutrient additives) or ground/surface water for toxicological investigations; natural sea water essential for marine organisms.

Dilution series prepared as geometric (progressive) concentration levels; a limit test needs no dilution series; a range-finding test with fewer organisms determines the approximate effective-concentration range.
Known reference substance used in the reference/control batch to monitor sensitivity and interferences, e.g. sodium dichromate or 3,5-dichlorophenol.

Number of parallel batches/replicates per concentration & control level for independent observations; at least two replicates recommended (control batches at least twice the replicates per concentration level or increased by sqrt(p)).

Threshold concentration determined: NOEC (no observed effect concentration) or LOEC (lowest observed effect concentration), via analysis of variance (ANOVA) and Dunnett's test; statistical determination detailed in §12.3.1.

Type of endpoint data: quantal (qualitative, e.g. mortality/immobility) or metric (quantitative, e.g. growth/biomass/reproduction), of decisive importance for the test & evaluation design (statistical handling per §12.3).

Mechanism by which sample components can be lost during the test: evaporation of volatiles, biodegradation, abiotic degradation (hydrolysis/photolysis), sorption to vessel/material, foaming, precipitation, flocculation; preventive measures applied.

Where adsorption is anticipated, vessels incubated for at least 30 min with the sample at the envisaged concentration before testing, then discarded, and new subsequently filled fresh batches prepared.
Test-system mode (static, semistatic or flow-through) selected to control losses through degradation/hydrolysis; flow-through/semistatic recommended for hydrolysable or degradable substances.

Where colour/light or high turbidity directly impedes cell growth, correction applied (separate measurement/test vessels, turbidity at a different wavelength, combination with oxygen consumption/production measurement, light-path/depth reduction) so the limiting effect can be distinguished from toxicity.

Type of biodegradation distinguished: primary degradation (substance loses specific properties) or ultimate degradation (full degradation to thermodynamically stable inorganic products -- CO2, water, mineral salts -- and new biomass).

Biodegradation test method group: ready biodegradability, inherent (potential) biodegradability, or simulation test (cross-refs ISO 7827/9408/9439/9887/10707/10708/11733/14592/14593/10634; ISO 15462 per OECD guidelines).
Concentration of the substance in the organism (e.g. whole body or specific tissue), input to the bioconcentration factor BCF (Eq.1).
Concentration of the substance in the surrounding medium (e.g. water) or another parameter (e.g. food), input to the bioconcentration factor BCF (Eq.1).
Uptake rate k1 of the substance into the organism (kinetic alternative for computing BCF = k1/k2, Eq.1).
Elimination rate k2 of the substance from the organism (used for BCF = k1/k2, Eq.1, and for the clearance time CT50 = log_e2/k2, Eq.2).

Bioconcentration factor = c1/c2 = k1/k2 (Eq.1), at specific times or under steady-state conditions (BCF_ss); steady state when three successive analyses >=2 days apart differ by <=+/-20 %; screened via log10 P_ow (BCF ~ 0,1 * P_ow for log P_ow 3-6).
Clearance time for 50 % elimination = log_e2/k2 (Eq.2), under a one-compartment first-order kinetics model.

log10 of the n-octanol/water partition coefficient P_ow, a measure of lipophilicity used for a preliminary estimation of bioaccumulation potential; not suitable for ions, surfactants, MW>700 substances, or highly lipophilic substances (log P_ow >6).

Genotoxic effect category: a) gene (point) mutation, b) chromosome mutation (visible structural change), c) genome mutation (change in total chromosome number, polyploidy); assessed in-vivo or in-vitro with metabolic activation (S9 fraction) where appropriate.
Statistical effect-concentration parameter reported: EC_x (x % effect), EC50 / LC50 (LC0/LC50/LC100, EC0/EC50/EC100), IC_x, NOEC, LOEC, or NEC (extrapolated to zero).

Statistical method for evaluating the concentration/response relationship: probit/logit/Weibull (quantal), least-squares/non-linear regression (metric), ANOVA with Dunnett's or Williams' test, Fisher's exact, Kruskal-Wallis with Bonferroni-Holm, Spearman-Kaerber / Moving Average / Fieller (confidence interval).

Confidence interval of the EC50/effect concentration calculated and reported (e.g. by the Fieller method, or approximated via Moving Average / Spearman-Kaerber when no other method applies); confidence ranges per ISO 8466.

Degree of degradation = percentage decrease in concentration of one or several parameters; result reported within a 10 % range; kinetics (lag phase for adaptation, half-life, 10-day window) described.

Concentration/response curve presented together with the test results in a graph (per Figure 2), giving a clear picture of the relationship and agreement with the model; confidence ranges shown where possible.

Confirmation the test report records all required items a)-n): laboratory name; date/period; test-method reference; test organism; test-material designation; sample pretreatment; data; chemical/physical data; deviations; evaluation method; test details; commentary; signatures of responsible investigator and quality controller.
Reference to the test method used (International Standard number), recorded in the test report.
Signature of the responsible investigator on the test report.
Signature of the quality controller on the test report, if appropriate.
Quality-assurance measures (preparatory phase, internal & external quality control, evaluation) documented; complete records and all relevant data on the course of the examination and QA stated.
All parts of the test method described as actually used, with a routine part and standard operating procedures (SOPs) referenced.
Internal quality control includes carrying out tests with reference substances and keeping control charts, plus instrument calibration, multiple determinations, plausibility control and validation.

Confirmation the case is in scope: NOT an estuary/coastal water, microbiological sampling, sediment/suspended-solids/biota, impounded reach, or passive surface-water sampling (each routed to ISO 19458 / ISO 5667-4 / ISO 5667-23).
Confirmation the applicable normative references were consulted: ISO 5667-1, ISO 5667-3, ISO 5667-11, ISO 5667-14, ISO 6107-2:2006.
Principal purpose of the river/stream sampling programme (Introduction examples a/b): assess water-quality suitability for a particular use, or assess the impact of human activities on water quality.
Type/technique of sampling per the §3 definitions: automatic (3.1), composite (3.2), continuous (3.3), discrete (3.4), incremental/gradual (3.5), isokinetic (3.6), random (3.8), systematic (3.14).
Type of flowing water body: river (3.9, natural body flowing continuously/intermittently to a sea/lake/etc.) or watercourse (3.12, like a river but generally smaller scale).
A detailed sampling strategy/plan has been elaborated (often based on a preliminary survey) before sampling, considering the §4 general and environmental-situation aspects.

Parameters to be analysed for each sampling point and the in-situ measurements to be carried out (e.g. temperature, dissolved oxygen, acidity, discharge), with the methods specified (§4 general aspects b,c).
Number and locations of sampling points at the sampling site (§4 general aspect e; see also §5.1).
The sampling depth(s) to be used (§4 environmental-situation aspect d); normally one depth suffices unless stratification is present (see §5.1.2).
Confirmation safety aspects of the sampling point have been considered in the plan (§4 environmental-situation aspect a; detailed in §15).
Record of the river-system characteristics influencing contaminant behaviour: temperature, turbidity, depth, velocity, turbulence, slope, changes in direction/cross-section, nature of the bed (§4).

A sampling-point file is kept recording directions to the site, detailed point location, sampling method and specific details (keys, H&S); any change to the designated point is discussed/agreed with the programme originator and recorded.

In watercourses near the coast, tidal influence on flow/quality/mixing should be considered; flow and water-depth measurements taken to indicate tidal state; sampling at different tidal states is usually necessary.
Whether determinants are homogeneously distributed across the water body at the site; if homogeneous any point suffices, otherwise the §5.1.4 multi-point approach applies or another site is sought.
When the site must be retained despite heterogeneity: about six samples spread across the part of the cross-section carrying ~90% of total flow (large rivers may need more lateral/vertical samples).
Heterogeneity-test samples should preferably be taken at at least three flows corresponding as closely as possible to expected minimum, modal and maximum flows during the test period.
Where possible, the sampling-site location defined by a reference coordinate per the international coordinate system in ISO 19112.
Whether mixing is relevant to the sampling regime; if so the sampling location and associated parameters should preferably be defined clearly before sampling begins.
Dimension of mixing considered: vertical (top-to-bottom), lateral (side-to-side) or longitudinal (levelling concentration peaks downstream) - all three should be considered in site/point selection.
Distance over which effluents mix vertically: most watercourses mix vertically within 100 m, or within a few hundred metres at most; normally one sampling depth then suffices.

When the effect of a tributary/effluent on quality in a reach is of interest, at least two sites are chosen: one just upstream of the confluence and one far enough downstream to ensure complete mixing.

Determinants suggested to be checked at each location to be tested for heterogeneity (where required for the routine programme): pH, conductivity, chlorine, ammonia, suspended solids, dissolved oxygen, colour, iron, chlorophyll, TOC, BOD.
Whether travel-time data (time for a water mass to move between two defined points) are required - relevant to lateral mixing, reaeration/self-purification, mean-flow velocity and location selection.
One of three principal travel-time determination methods: surface floats (ISO 748), tracers (ISO 9555), or discharge measurement with known cross-section areas (ISO 748 & ISO 1070).
Travel-time measurements should be made at a minimum of five different flows, with resulting travel times plotted against corresponding flows for interpolation/extrapolation.
Extrapolation beyond 10% of a flow-measurement value can give incorrect travel-time information; keep extrapolation within 10%.
The programme is adequately statistically designed so the summary statistics estimate the required information within the objectives' tolerance limits (apply ISO 5667-1 statistics guidance).
The objectives include a definition of the magnitude of acceptable error; without it a statistics-based sampling programme is not possible.
Sampling strategy: systematic (preferred for better mean-estimate precision when cyclic/persistent variations are present, given a short-enough interval) or random.
When using systematic sampling, the sampling frequency does not coincide with any natural cycle in the system or other time-based effect (e.g. an hourly upstream pump).
If the programme is designed to detect trends, it uses fixed sampling points and standardized methodologies to a set programme so all variations of interest are detected.
All sampling personnel are properly trained and given clear sampling instructions; lone working is avoided in favour of teamwork; operators and vehicles are self-contained.

The minimum information set (§6 a-e) is available: precise point description/documentation; type of sample required; applicable protocols/techniques; sub-sample info (bottles, filtration, preservation, field measurements); order of filling containers.
A cooling device in the vehicle capable of keeping samples at (5 +/- 3) degC for transport (i.e. 2-8 degC).
The vehicle is equipped with racking to hold equipment and prevent movement that could cause breakage (important for glass bottles, preservative bottles and hand meters).
Type of specific sampling location: from a bridge (§7.2), in the watercourse by wading (§7.3), from the bank (§7.4), from a boat (§7.5) or under ice (§7.6).
When sampling from a bridge, whether the sample is taken upstream or downstream of the bridge (Tab.1 lists the advantages/disadvantages of each); collection is preferably upstream in the main flow.

The four §7.2 bridge-site checks (a-d) are satisfied: sufficient water depth to submerge the container; container does not disturb bed deposits; sufficient clearance to avoid detachment/contamination; operator not left without view on the upstream side.
Where possible, samples are collected about 30 cm below the surface (or otherwise mid-way between bed and surface), avoiding the surface film and eddies (§7.3, §7.4, §7.5, §10.4).
Samples obtained from positions at least 30 cm above the bed of a watercourse (and a similar distance below the surface) are usually satisfactory; avoid disturbing bottom sediments.
Personal protective equipment (high-visibility jackets) and flotation equipment (life-jackets) should be used if appropriate when sampling at specific locations (see §15).
Verbatim recommendation that samples be collected about 30 cm below the surface; input to the recommended-depth relation (Eq.2).
Sampling method used: single discrete grab (§8.1), sampling from a specific depth (§8.2) or a continuous sampling system (§8.2/§9.4).
Range of sampling flasks to be employed: 50 ml to 3 L; larger volumes may be needed to reach analytical detection limits for clean rivers (handling problems may then arise).
For continuous sampling systems where isokinetic conditions are not possible, the linear flow velocity within the inlet tube shall be not less than 0,5 m/s nor greater than 3,0 m/s.

For representative sampling of insoluble materials, sampling is carried out under isokinetic conditions (inlet velocity equal to the stream velocity, inlet facing the flow direction). Ideal where achievable.

All equipment/devices are, as far as possible, of materials inert to the components to be analysed, and are tested before use to demonstrate no effect on the determinand; properly maintained and cleaned.
Operating mode of an automatic sampler: preset time intervals, external trigger (e.g. excessive-rainfall signal), or flow-proportional (samples after a fixed volume has passed).
All equipment contacting the water is washed, preferably up to three times, with water from the body to be sampled (do not rinse bottles that contain preservatives).

Procedure used to take the sample: direct (§10.4, lowest contamination risk; not with preservative-bottles), indirect via dip flask (§10.5), through ice (§10.6), surface film (§10.7) or incremental (§10.8).
For a sample regarded as single/discrete prepared from increments, the total time for all increments should be such that no change in river composition is expected; if unknown, less than 5 min.

Whether preservatives are added in the field (required for certain sample types, e.g. dissolved oxygen) per ISO 5667-3 and specific analytical standards, following manufacturer instructions and using appropriate PPE.
Samples are labelled (per §12.2) at the time of collection and before moving to the next sampling site; no further samples collected until all bottles are labelled.
Risk factors that could contaminate/affect the sample are excluded as far as possible and indicated on the sampling form (environmental, method/procedure and sampling-material factors per §10.1).
Samples are stabilized/preserved according to ISO 5667-3 and the appropriate analytical standards; all preservation steps and the storage temperature are recorded.

For soluble-species applications (e.g. dissolved trace metals), dissolved material is separated from particulate as soon as possible after sampling, preferably by on-site filtration (details in ISO 5667-3).
The storage temperature is measured and recorded as part of the preservation record.
The operator maintains security and traceability of samples, sub-samples and sample records; condition checked and samples deposited in the designated place; any loss/damage/breakage recorded.

Whether samples may be used for legal purposes; if so, the (potentially far more complex) regulations of the applicable jurisdiction shall be followed and all involved persons fully familiar with the local legislation.
Specific written instructions on contamination-avoidance protocols are provided to sampling personnel for surface-water sampling; deviations from anticipated risks are documented.

Sampling operators use disposable gloves throughout the sampling procedure to protect from contact with the sample and to prevent contaminating the sample (avoiding cross-contamination between sites).
Sample containers are clearly and unambiguously identified via a label affixed to the container so subsequent analytical results can be correctly interpreted.
Quality-control/assurance techniques (training, equipment calibration, data logging, blanks for cross-contamination) per ISO 5667-14 are applied; strongly recommended to optimize result quality.

The sampling report includes the applicable §13.1 items (a-q): river name; sampling point; specific-location info; date/time; collector; weather/air temp; water-body appearance/condition/temp; flow condition; sample appearance; device type; preservation; filtration; storage; deviations; in-situ measurements; collector notes; reference to ISO 5667-6.
Individual analytical-report item from the §13.1 a-q list (enumerated as Enum_Values).

enum_values.label_en: Flow condition of the water body

description: A history of changes to sampling procedures/protocols (methods, points, personnel) is kept so a data examiner can assess the impact of changes on the observation series.

A quality-management system (e.g. ISO/IEC 17025) is developed/adopted/applied; the system does not itself specify data quality - that is defined by the data's purpose and specified by the data user before sampling.
Personal safety problems are always assessed for each sampling event and, where appropriate, an on-site risk assessment is carried out.
Personal protective equipment is provided - flotation equipment, a depth pole/rod and high-visibility clothing - to ensure safety. Waders are not used (they present a safety risk).

Outcome of the §15 risk assessment: do not sample at all; sample only if securely attached to an adequate anchor point; sample only if a second person is present with harness and ropes; or safe to proceed.

Whether an unsafe condition is present in which sampling shall not be attempted: doubtful ice thickness/load capacity or no ice training; severe weather (heavy rain/snow, slip/landslide risk); remote areas with compromised/no communications.
Annex A Eq.(A.1) output: approximate distance (m) for complete mixing within 1% of full homogeneity.
Annex A: reach mean width, expressed in metres (m).
Annex A: Chezy coefficient for the reach (15 < c < 50). Example uses c=15 (rough/turbulent) and c=50 (smooth/slow).
Annex A: acceleration due to gravity, expressed in metres per second squared (m/s^2).
Annex A: reach mean depth, expressed in metres (m).

label_en: Position within the value chain or value network
description: Where the organization's solutions fit in the value chain/network; prerequisite before implementing actions (6.1).

label_en: Commitment to contribute to a circular economy
description: Organization seeks to understand and commit or contribute to a circular economy while contributing to sustainable development.
Identity of the organization seeking to commit/contribute to a circular economy.
Private or public; individual or collective; regardless of type or size.
Jurisdiction in which the organization is located.
System defined by selected boundaries, subject of a circularity measurement/assessment (regional, interorganizational, organizational, product).
Element of an organization's activities/solutions that interacts with the circular economy (durability, recyclability, reusability, repairability, recoverability).
Selector over the 23 circular-economy terms (3.1); supportive vocabulary lookup.
Long-term vision: reduced, efficient, effective use of resources and prevention of harmful releases/losses/degradation when meeting societal needs; decoupling growth from resource consumption.
Systems thinking should be applied to circular economy activities (Clause 4 / 5.2.1).
The six principles (Clause 5) should be integrated into organizational strategies and objectives.
Focusing on only one or two principles can undermine achievements; integrating all six is important (5.3.2).
A risk-based approach should be used to avoid exposure to hazardous substances; where possible organizations should avoid their use.
Organization identifies and measures use of all resource types and traces mass and value over time; monitors losses by type, disposition and effects.
One of the six interlinked principles considered for the transition; all should be considered together.
Grouping of actions: added value, value retention, value recovery, ecosystem regeneration, transition support.

enum_values.label_en: Actions that contribute to value retention
Actions that contribute to value recovery
Actions to support a circular economy transition

description: Organizations should consider refuse and rethink as preliminary actions.
A life cycle perspective should guide the identification of the best action for the value creation model and to avoid unwanted trade-offs.
In general, products should be repaired before remanufactured, and remanufactured before recycled - unless a life cycle perspective yields a better outcome.
Action chosen from the R-strategy hierarchy (refuse->re-mine), prioritized via a life cycle perspective.
Stage of the iterative implementation process (Figure 4): context assessment, purpose/goals, strategy/action plan, implementation, monitoring.

enum_values.label_en: Purpose, mission, vision and goals definition
Strategic priorities and action plan development

description: System level at which the organization operates: global/regional/country/local, interorganizational, organizational (product covered indirectly).
Organization should determine its reference situation regarding a circular economy (current practices, resource flows, alignment with principles).
Selected circularity indicators should be calculated and a baseline circularity assessment performed (methods owned by ISO 59020).
Indicator chosen to assess effectiveness/efficiency of interventions and monitor progress; determined with the principles, goals and strategic priorities in mind.

label_en: Circular economy purpose, mission and vision
description: Purpose, mission and vision developed in alignment with the circular economy principles; should inspire change and provide clear direction.
Goals with intermediate targets to allow circularity assessments of progress from the reference situation towards longer-term goals.
Strategy linking mission, vision, goals, priorities, targets and respective actions/projects followed by a measuring framework and a set of circularity indicators.
Action plan for how the strategy will be implemented; scope, responsibilities, capabilities, timeline, potential setbacks.
Dimension against which actions are assessed for feasibility: technical, organizational, financial/economic, context, social, environmental.
Preliminary pilot application of a specific practice/segment to ensure it works as planned and risks/barriers are addressed before wider implementation.
Value creation model aligned with the circular economy; explored to address identified opportunities to create value.
Organization should choose circularity indicators and often review indicators and circularity performance to set the basis for continual improvement.
The organization seeking to transition its value creation models and value networks from linear to circular; applicable to any organization regardless of size, sector or region (§1).
Edition of ISO 59010 applied (ISO/FDIS 59010:2024).

Organization's chosen system of interconnected and interdependent decisions and activities that determines how it creates, delivers and captures value; typically linear at the start of the transition (§3.1).
Where the organization's solution fits in the value chain (e.g. manufacturer upstream, service provider downstream); the set of organizations that provide a solution resulting in value (§3.17, §A.1).

Goal the organization seeks to achieve by transitioning to a circular economy value creation model (e.g. reductions in resource inflows/outflows, energy and water consumption, improved resource efficiency) (§4.1).
To set measurable goals, the organization conducts an assessment by reviewing and mapping all its activities and interactions within and between its value chains and broader value network (§4.1).

label_en: Goal defined early in solution development
description: Defining the goals early in the solution development process enables circularity aspects to be incorporated in the design of the solution (§4.1).
Typical business element constituting the organization's current value creation model, assessed to understand the model (§4.2 a-j).

validation_rules.raw: business_element IN {value_proposition, key_activities, key_business_resources, customer_segment, customer_relationships, channels, costs, revenue_streams, key_partners, other_elements}

description: In addition to the business elements, relevant enablers should be identified and understood for how their availability influences business elements (§4.2).
The organization should map its existing relationships with other organizations and interested parties up and down the value chain along with associated resource flows (§4.3).
Mapping can be applied through qualitative or quantitative stakeholder analysis with the participation of interested parties (§4.3).
Organizations should assess whether there are sufficient enablers (shared infrastructure, circular suppliers, academic partnerships, R&D) or if others need to be developed (§4.3).
Setting the boundary (e.g. a company or group of companies within the value network) clarifies the scope of actions; this boundary applies to all following clauses and subclauses (§4.4).

The boundary should include all relevant activities, locations, types of solutions and value networks, and the portion of the economic system within which the organization operates, collaborates or exercises influence (§4.4).

label_en: Boundary aligned with sphere of influence
description: To set an appropriate boundary, an organization should consider its sphere of influence and align the boundary with the boundary of its ambition (§4.4, §3.15).
Understanding current circularity performance by selecting circularity KPIs and using them to assess the current value creation model and value network within the boundary (§4.5).
ISO 59020 indicator category used to assess circular performance: resource inflows, resource outflows, energy, water, economic (§4.5).

validation_rules.raw: indicator_category IN {resource_inflows, resource_outflows, energy, water, economic}

description: Use the selected KPIs to assess the state of the current value creation model and value network, to ensure the defined goals are appropriate (§4.5).
Methodology for assessing circular performance, e.g. full or streamlined LCA, eco-efficiency assessment, water footprint assessment or others referenced in ISO 59020 (§4.5 NOTE 2).

label_en: Refuse & rethink considered as preliminary actions
description: Organizations should consider refuse and rethink as preliminary actions before other actions (§4.6.1).
Action that creates added value, selected from §4.6.2: design for circularity, circular sourcing, circular procurement, process optimization, industrial/regional/urban symbiosis.

validation_rules.raw: added_value_action IN {design_for_circularity, circular_sourcing, circular_procurement, process_optimization, industrial_regional_urban_symbiosis}

label_en: Action that contributes to value retention
description: Action that contributes to value retention, selected from §4.6.3: reduce/reuse/repurpose, maintenance & repair, performance-based approaches, sharing to intensify use, refurbishing, remanufacturing.

validation_rules.raw: value_retention_action IN {reduce_reuse_repurpose, maintenance_repair, performance_based_approaches, sharing_to_intensify_use, refurbishing, remanufacturing}

label_en: Action that contributes to value recovery
description: Action that contributes to value recovery, selected from §4.6.4: reverse logistics, cascading (technical/biobased), recycling, waste management, material recovery, energy recovery.

validation_rules.raw: value_recovery_action IN {reverse_logistics, cascading_technical, cascading_biobased, recycling, waste_management, material_recovery, energy_recovery}

description: Actions to regenerate degraded ecosystems (removal of harmful substances, remediation, climate mitigation/adaptation, biodiversity protection, regenerative production) to align with the ecosystem resilience principle (§4.6.5).

label_en: Action to support a circular economy transition
description: Enabling action to support the transition, selected from §4.6.6: education & research, innovation, collaboration & networks, helping users change behaviour, policy & legal system, financial services, digitalization.

validation_rules.raw: transition_support_action IN {education_research, innovation, collaboration_networks, helping_users_change_behaviour, policy_legal_system, financial_services, digitalization}

description: Resource management action prioritized per Table 2 with a life cycle perspective: refuse, rethink, source, reduce, repair, re-use, refurbish, remanufacture, repurpose, cascade, recycle, recover energy, re-mine (§4.6.7, Table 2).

validation_rules.raw: resource_management_action IN {refuse, rethink, source, reduce, repair, re_use, refurbish, remanufacture, repurpose, cascade, recycle, recover_energy, re_mine}

description: A life cycle perspective should guide the organization in identifying the best action for its value creation model and to avoid unwanted trade-offs; in general, repair before remanufacture before recycle (§4.6.7).

The organization should identify the gaps and opportunities to transition its value creation model towards circularity by evaluating the value creation model elements against the circular economy principles (§5.1, Figure 4).

ISO 59004 circular economy principle on which the strategy is based: systems thinking, value creation, value sharing, resource stewardship, resource traceability, ecosystem resilience (§5.2, Figure 4).

validation_rules.raw: circular_economy_principle IN {systems_thinking, value_creation, value_sharing, resource_stewardship, resource_traceability, ecosystem_resilience}

description: Strategy for the transition of the value creation model and value network to achieve the goals, determined by considering purpose/vision/mission, gaps & opportunities, repositioning and sphere of influence (§5.2).

Materiality is a key consideration; organizations conduct materiality assessments (e.g. a materiality matrix of interested-party expectations vs business priorities) to support strategy decisions (§5.2, §3.8, §3.9).
The transition cannot successfully be conducted without economic rationalization; all value creation models presume an ability to realize a profit while accounting for risks (§5.3).

Plan to shift from the current to the desired future value creation model, including objectives, timelines, actions and anticipated interim results expressed in KPIs, aligned with the strategy (§6.1).
The objectives and interim results should be expressed in KPIs used to assess the status of circularity (4.6) and the plan should be in line with the circular economy strategy (5.2) (§6.1).

A value proposition for circularity includes fulfilling the target group's needs while keeping resources at their highest value as long as possible (e.g. via reuse, repair, remanufacturing, recycling, PSS) (§6.2.2).
As a key business resource, recovered resources (via reusing/recycling products, parts or materials) take precedence over virgin resources extracted from the earth (§6.2.4).

The organization should consider changes to each value creation model element consistent with the developed plan (value proposition, key activities/resources, customers, channels, costs, revenue, key partners, external) (§6.2.1-§6.2.11).

Additional potential risk/opportunity to explore: current/future compliance obligations, end-to-end processes (life cycle), market/societal perspectives, unintended consequences, use of renewable energy, education & awareness (§6.2.12).

enum_values.label_en: Current solutions related to end-to-end processes (life cycle perspective)
Market and societal perspectives of linear value networks
Potential unintended consequences from circular economy solutions
Education and awareness of circular economy objectives

validation_rules.raw: other_consideration IN {compliance_obligations, end_to_end_processes, market_societal_perspectives, unintended_consequences, renewable_energy_use, education_awareness}

description: Value network members should determine their shared objectives by considering symbiotic opportunities and members' individual circular objectives (§7.2).
Members can create a shared circular economy strategy and a shared plan with timelines and expected interim results to shift their value networks towards circularity (§7.2).
Participating members should engage in consistency verification to ensure alignment in objectives, values, governance and decision-making throughout the network (§7.2).

A governance structure should be implemented in a value network (e.g. forum, alliance, pacts, consortium, members networks, public-private partnerships), considering the §7.3 governance elements (§7.3).
During the transition it is often necessary to expand the project's boundary beyond the organization's immediate value chain to develop circular flows of resources through collaboration (§7.1).

Element to be considered for value-network governance per §7.3 (clear roles & responsibilities, respect for member liberty, advisory/steering body, shared by-laws, communication channels, risk management, trust-building, transparent decision-making, traceability mechanisms, reporting/non-financial disclosure).

enum_values.label_en: Clear roles and responsibilities of members

enum_values.label_de: Respekt fuer die Freiheit der Mitglieder
enum_values.label_en: Respect for the liberty and free will of each member
Advisory group, steering committee or governing board
Shared by-laws providing principles and rules
Clear and active communication channels and protocols
Reporting processes to interested parties (esp. non-financial disclosure)

validation_rules.raw: governance_element IN {clear_roles_responsibilities, respect_member_liberty, advisory_or_steering_body, shared_by_laws, communication_channels, risk_management, trust_building, transparent_decision_making, traceability_mechanisms, reporting_to_parties}

description: Shared physical/digital infrastructure component leveraged or established: information exchange platform (e.g. blockchain, digital material/product passports), shared facilities & assets (reverse logistics, warehouses, PCM treatment, land/energy recovery), leveraged knowledge & skills (§7.4).
After selecting actions to improve circularity, the organization should measure and assess the results as its circularity performance, aligned with the KPIs described in 4.5 (§8.1).

Measurement and assessment of circularity performance should be meaningful: the data needs to be relevant and precise enough for the intended application, including all resource inflows/outflows (incl. emissions and losses) via ISO 59020 core indicators (§8.1).
Complementary method for assessing impacts on social/environmental/economic aspects, e.g. ISO 14044 for LCA, ISO 26000 for social responsibility (§8.1).
The outcome is specific to a defined time period; to monitor progress over time the organization can choose to carry out periodic assessments (§8.1).
At an appropriate interval, review the plan (6.1) from the perspectives of achieved performance, value creation model elements (4.2, 6.2) and access to finance and funding (§8.2).

At an appropriate interval, review the shared strategic plan (7.2) transparently/inclusively/impartially from the perspectives of performance, boundary expansion, member diversity, member relationships and governance performance/structure (§8.3).
The organization (person or group with its own functions, responsibilities, authorities and relationships) applying the requirements of this document (§3.17).
Edition of ISO 59014 applied (ISO/DIS 59014:2023, Draft International Standard).

The activity/process for recovering secondary materials in focus that the standard applies to: collection, classification, sorting, non-destructive process, destructive process, logistics (§1 scope; enumerated in §5.1, Figure 3).

validation_rules.raw: recovery_activity_in_focus IN {collection, classification, sorting, non_destructive_process, destructive_process, logistics}

description: Principle of this document considered/applied (§4.2.1-4.2.8). All eight principles are the basis for the requirements (§4.1).

enum_values.label_de: Respekt fuer Interessen der interessierten Parteien

enum_values.label_en: Responsibility towards interested parties engaged in subsistence activities
Safe, healthy, and equitable working conditions
Enabling of circular resource flow using secondary materials

validation_rules.raw: principle_considered IN {respect_for_interested_parties, value_chain_responsibility, responsibility_towards_sa, safe_healthy_equitable_working_conditions, protection_of_the_environment, resource_conservation, life_cycle_perspective, enabling_circular_resource_flow}

label_en: Principles applied in a true, fair and consistent manner
description: The principles shall be applied so that the achievement and demonstration of sustainability and traceability is undertaken in a true, fair and consistent manner (§4.1).

Type and sequence of activities and processes applied to recover products, components and materials from recoverable resources (§3.20); determined by how recoverable resources are collected and classified (§5.2).

label_en: Organization type in the recovery chain
description: Type of organization involved in recovery: collector, dismantler, re-processor, remanufacturer, refiner, etc. (§5.3; examples in informative Annex A).
